questions.q: Per this lesson's comparison matrix, what actually tracks the pattern choice more tightly than data volume does?
options: The number of Apex classes required to implement the integration
The primary risk if that integration fails -- which cases call for near-instant, synchronous handling versus which can tolerate real delay
Which case study was built first chronologically
The number of fields shared between the two systems
questions.explain: The lesson shows that failure-risk severity, not raw data volume, is what actually explains why the identity-provider case (low volume) needed synchronous handling while the data-warehouse case (high volume) could tolerate hours of staleness.

questions.q: Why does the identity-provider case use a synchronous, real-time pattern despite having the lowest data volume of the five cases?
options: Low-volume integrations are always built synchronously by convention
Its failure mode -- a user being locked out of Salesforce entirely -- is immediately disruptive, so near-instant handling is required regardless of the low data volume
SAML cannot technically be implemented asynchronously under any circumstances
Identity providers always require more data volume than ERPs
questions.explain: The pattern choice follows the failure-risk column, not the volume column -- a total login lockout demands real-time handling even though the actual data volume involved is small.

questions.q: Why is the data-warehouse case comfortable with a multi-hour freshness window, per this lesson's matrix?
options: Because the Bulk API is physically incapable of running more than once per day
Because its failure mode -- a dashboard being a few hours stale -- is tolerable in a way the other four cases' failure modes are not
Because data warehouses never need current data under any circumstances
Because Salesforce prohibits more frequent syncs to data warehouses
questions.explain: The warehouse case's tolerance for delay comes from its failure mode being mild (stale reporting) compared to cases like the portal, where the failure mode (wrong customer seeing another's data) is severe regardless of delay.

questions.q: What specific weakness does this lesson identify in a design process that only asks 'how much data' and skips 'what happens if this breaks'?
options: It would have reached worse answers for at least two of the five cases, since volume alone doesn't predict failure-risk severity
It would produce identical answers to the risk-based process in every case
It is the correct and sufficient process, and risk doesn't need separate consideration
It only applies to cases involving external identity providers
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly notes that volume alone would have suggested different priorities than risk-of-failure did, producing worse answers for cases like identity (low volume, high risk) and the warehouse (high volume, low risk).

questions.q: Why does a review board typically care about an explicit comparison matrix rather than five separate, case-by-case justifications?
options: Because review boards only grade on the number of pages submitted
Because the matrix demonstrates one consistent decision process applied across all cases, rather than appearing to be five disconnected, ad hoc answers
Because comparison matrices are a mandatory Salesforce certification requirement
Because review boards never ask about failure risk, only about data volume
questions.explain: A review board probing consistency wants to see the same criteria applied across cases that look superficially similar but got different answers -- the matrix is what shows that consistency transparently.
